subtopics.name: Increased intracranial pressure and head injury

questions.stem: A client has had a stroke in the right cerebral hemisphere. Which finding should the nurse expect?

options.text: Left-sided weakness, impulsive behavior and neglect of the left side
Loss of the ability to read and write

rationale.correct: Right-brain stroke: left-sided weakness, neglect, impulsivity and poor judgment, so safety is the main concern. Left-brain stroke: right-sided weakness, aphasia and slow, cautious behavior.

perOption.a: These occur with left hemisphere strokes.
perOption.b: Right hemisphere damage affects the left side of the body, spatial awareness and judgment.
perOption.c: Cautious behavior is typical of left hemisphere strokes.
perOption.d: Language deficits are usually from left hemisphere damage.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Predict deficits after a right hemisphere stroke.

questions.stem: A client with expressive (Broca's) aphasia understands what is said but has trouble speaking. Which communication strategy is best?

options.text: Ask yes-or-no questions and offer a picture or communication board
Avoid talking to the client to prevent frustration

rationale.correct: Expressive aphasia: comprehension is intact, speech isn't. Give time and use simple questions and aids.

perOption.a: The client's hearing isn't the problem.
perOption.b: These let the client communicate without needing fluent speech.
perOption.c: This can frustrate the client and discourage attempts to speak.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Communicate with a client who has expressive aphasia.

questions.stem: A client arrives with sudden right-sided weakness and slurred speech that began 1 hour ago. Which test should the nurse expect first?

options.text: Non-contrast CT scan of the head

rationale.correct: Get a non-contrast head CT immediately to tell ischemic from hemorrhagic stroke.

perOption.a: A CT quickly rules out hemorrhage before thrombolytic therapy.
perOption.b: An MRI takes longer and isn't the usual first test.
perOption.c: This isn't the initial stroke test.
perOption.d: This is done later to find the cause.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify the first diagnostic test for a suspected stroke.

questions.stem: A client with an acute ischemic stroke is a candidate for alteplase. The blood pressure is 196/112 mm Hg. What should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Lowering the blood pressure below 185/110 before giving alteplase
Lowering the blood pressure to below 120/80

rationale.correct: Before alteplase, keep BP below 185/110; after it, keep BP below 180/105 for 24 hours.

perOption.a: Blood pressure must be below 185/110 before alteplase.
perOption.b: High blood pressure raises the risk of bleeding into the brain.
perOption.c: Rapid lowering can extend the stroke.
perOption.d: This pressure is too high for thrombolysis.

references: American Heart Association Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: After a stroke, a client has homonymous hemianopsia on the left. Which intervention is most appropriate?

options.text: Place the meal tray and call light on the client's left side
Teach the client to turn the head to scan the left side
Approach the client from the left

rationale.correct: Hemianopsia: place items in the intact field at first and teach scanning toward the lost side.

perOption.a: The client can't see the left visual field.
perOption.b: Scanning makes up for the lost visual field.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with left-sided neglect after a stroke ignores the left arm. Which intervention should the nurse include?

options.text: Dress the client's unaffected side first
Remind the client to look at and touch the left arm and position it safely
Keep the left arm under the covers
Ignore the neglect, because it will resolve on its own

rationale.correct: Unilateral neglect: cue the client to attend to the affected side and protect the limb.

perOption.a: The affected side is dressed first.
perOption.b: Cueing the client increases awareness and prevents injury to the neglected limb.
perOption.c: This increases neglect and the risk of injury.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: Which findings are warning signs of a stroke that should prompt the client's family to call 911? Select all that apply.

options.text: Sudden vision loss or double vision
Drooping of one side of the face

rationale.correct: BE-FAST: Balance, Eyes, Face, Arm, Speech, Time to call 911.

perOption.a: B in BE-FAST: balance.
perOption.b: E: eyes.

references: American Heart Association Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach the warning signs of stroke.

questions.stem: Which finding is the earliest sign of increasing intracranial pressure?

options.text: Change in level of consciousness, such as restlessness or confusion
Bradycardia and a widened pulse pressure

rationale.correct: A change in LOC is the earliest sign of rising ICP.

perOption.a: The level of consciousness is the most sensitive early indicator.
perOption.b: This is a late sign.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with a head injury has a blood pressure that has risen from 138/80 to 184/70 mm Hg, a heart rate that has fallen from 88 to 52/min and irregular breathing. What do these findings indicate?

options.text: Cushing's triad, a late sign of increased ICP

rationale.correct: Cushing's triad: hypertension with widening pulse pressure, bradycardia and irregular respirations. Notify the provider immediately.

perOption.a: Widening pulse pressure, bradycardia and irregular respirations signal impending herniation.
perOption.b: Shock causes hypotension and tachycardia.
perOption.c: Neurogenic shock causes hypotension and bradycardia.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: Which interventions help reduce intracranial pressure? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keep the head of the bed at 30 degrees
Keep the head in a midline position

rationale.correct: Lower ICP by promoting venous drainage and avoiding activities that raise intrathoracic or abdominal pressure.

perOption.a: This promotes venous drainage from the brain.
perOption.b: Turning the head can block the jugular veins.
perOption.c: Hip flexion raises abdominal and intracranial pressure.
perOption.d: Clustering many activities can raise ICP.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with cerebral edema is receiving IV mannitol. Which assessment is most important?

options.text: Serum osmolality, urine output and signs of fluid and electrolyte imbalance

rationale.correct: Mannitol: monitor osmolality (hold if above about 320 mOsm/kg), urine output, electrolytes and signs of heart failure. Use an in-line filter.

perOption.a: Mannitol is an osmotic diuretic; it can cause dehydration, electrolyte shifts and kidney injury.
perOption.b: This isn't the main concern.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with a head injury has clear fluid draining from the nose and bruising behind the ears. Which action should the nurse avoid?

options.text: Nasotracheal suctioning or inserting a nasogastric tube
Checking the drainage for a halo sign
Raising the head of the bed

rationale.correct: Basal skull fracture: Battle sign (bruising behind the ear), raccoon eyes and CSF leak. Nothing goes in through the nose.

perOption.a: These suggest a basal skull fracture; tubes through the nose can enter the brain.
perOption.b: A halo on gauze suggests CSF.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Avoid nasal tubes in suspected basal skull fracture.

questions.stem: A client was briefly unconscious after a fall, then woke and talked normally. Two hours later, the client is hard to wake and has a dilated right pupil. What does the nurse suspect?

rationale.correct: An epidural hematoma is a neurosurgical emergency.

perOption.a: A brief loss of consciousness, a lucid interval, then rapid decline is typical of arterial bleeding.
perOption.b: A concussion doesn't cause a delayed decline with pupil changes.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client opens the eyes only to painful stimuli, uses inappropriate words and withdraws from pain. What is the Glasgow Coma Scale score?

rationale.correct: Eye opening to pain = 2. Verbal: inappropriate words = 3. Motor: withdraws from pain = 4. Total = 9.
references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Calculate a Glasgow Coma Scale score.

questions.stem: A client with a mild concussion is being discharged. Which statement shows a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I'll come back if I keep vomiting or my headache gets worse."
"I'll have someone stay with me for the first 24 hours."
"I can go back to playing football this weekend if I feel okay."

rationale.correct: Concussion: watch for red flags, rest and return gradually to activity with clearance.

perOption.a: These are warning signs.
perOption.b: Observation is recommended.
perOption.c: Return to contact sports requires gradual progression and medical clearance.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach a client after a concussion.

questions.stem: A client has been having one tonic-clonic seizure after another for 6 minutes without waking in between. Which medication should the nurse prepare to give first?

rationale.correct: Status epilepticus: protect the airway, give a benzodiazepine (IV lorazepam, or IM midazolam), then a second-line drug.

perOption.a: A benzodiazepine is first-line for status epilepticus.
perOption.b: Oral drugs aren't effective during a seizure.
perOption.c: This is second-line, after a benzodiazepine.
perOption.d: Oral drugs aren't used in an emergency.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: After a client's seizure, what is most important for the nurse to document?

options.text: Time it started, how long it lasted, the body parts involved and the client's condition afterward
What the client ate that day

rationale.correct: Document onset, duration, progression, type of movements, level of consciousness, incontinence and the post-ictal state.

perOption.a: These details help identify the seizure type and guide treatment.
perOption.b: This isn't enough.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is giving phenytoin IV. Which action is correct?

options.text: Give it with 0.9% sodium chloride, no faster than 50 mg/min, and monitor the ECG and blood pressure
Give it as a rapid IV push

rationale.correct: IV phenytoin: saline only, slow rate, an in-line filter and cardiac monitoring.

perOption.a: Phenytoin precipitates in dextrose.
perOption.b: Phenytoin is compatible only with saline; rapid infusion can cause hypotension and dysrhythmias.
perOption.c: IM phenytoin is erratic and damages tissue.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client's phenytoin level is 28 mcg/mL (therapeutic range 10 to 20). Which finding should the nurse expect?

options.text: Nystagmus, unsteady gait and slurred speech

rationale.correct: Phenytoin toxicity: nystagmus, ataxia, slurred speech and confusion. Long-term effects include gingival hyperplasia.

perOption.a: These are signs of phenytoin toxicity.
perOption.b: Toxicity causes sedation.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client is starting levetiracetam for seizures. Which statement shows a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I'll tell my provider if I feel depressed or have thoughts of hurting myself."
"I'll stop the medicine once my seizures stop."
"I won't drive until my provider says it's safe."

rationale.correct: Never stop antiseizure drugs suddenly; watch for mood changes.

perOption.a: Antiseizure drugs carry a warning about mood changes and suicidal thoughts.
perOption.b: Stopping suddenly can trigger seizures, including status epilepticus.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach a client about antiseizure medication.

questions.stem: A client has fever, headache and a stiff neck. When the nurse flexes the client's neck, the client's hips and knees flex. What does this finding indicate?

options.text: Positive Brudzinski sign, suggesting meningeal irritation

rationale.correct: Signs of meningeal irritation: nuchal rigidity, Brudzinski sign and Kernig sign.

perOption.a: This finding suggests meningitis.
perOption.b: Babinski involves the toes fanning out when the sole is stroked.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client is admitted with suspected bacterial (meningococcal) meningitis. Which precautions should the nurse put in place?

options.text: Droplet precautions until 24 hours of effective antibiotics

rationale.correct: Meningococcal meningitis: droplet precautions until 24 hours of antibiotics; close contacts may need prophylaxis.

perOption.a: Meningococcus spreads by respiratory droplets.
perOption.b: Meningococcus isn't airborne.

references: CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: How should the nurse position a client for a lumbar puncture?

options.text: Side-lying with the knees drawn up and the chin tucked
Prone with a pillow under the head

rationale.correct: Lumbar puncture: fetal position (or sitting and leaning forward); afterward, encourage fluids and watch for headache.

perOption.a: Curving the spine widens the spaces between the vertebrae.
perOption.b: This doesn't open the spaces.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Position a client for a lumbar puncture.

questions.stem: Which posture indicates the most severe brain dysfunction?

options.text: Decorticate posturing (arms flexed toward the chest)

rationale.correct: Decerebrate (extension) is worse than decorticate (flexion).

perOption.a: Extension posturing indicates brainstem damage and a worse prognosis.
perOption.b: This indicates damage higher in the brain and is less severe.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with hypertension calls the nurse. Highlight the findings that require emergency evaluation for a possible hemorrhagic stroke.

segments.text: a sudden, severe headache, "the worst of my life"
taking blood pressure medication this morning

rationale.correct: A sudden, severe headache with vomiting and neck stiffness needs emergency evaluation for hemorrhage.

perOption.s2: A thunderclap headache suggests subarachnoid hemorrhage.
perOption.s4: Vomiting with a sudden headache suggests raised ICP.
perOption.s6: Blood in the subarachnoid space irritates the meninges.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Reviewed by the content team on 17 November 2026.
